# Diagnosis Before Recovery: Turning Agent Failures into Selective Self-Correction

- **Authors**: Pan Wang, Yihao Hu, Hang Wang, Zirui Lv, Xin Zhang, Jianshe Li, Jiang-Ming Yang, Wei Wu, Yongqi Tong
- **Venue**: cs.CL
- **Published**: 2026-08-12
- **Source**: arxiv
- **Link**: <https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.11772>
- **PDF**: <https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.11772v1>
- **Topics**: test-time-scaling
- **Relevance score**: test-time-scaling 0.50

## In one line

Profiles the dominant failure mode of an agent task family on development data, then freezes a policy that permits only the recovery interventions matched to that failure -- so a failure decides which repair is admissible and how much evidence to spend, rather than triggering more context indiscriminately.

## Problem

Coding agents self-correct well because compilers, tests and traces make a failure actionable: a type error, a failing assertion and a timeout call for different repairs and the environment distinguishes them. Most agent benchmarks supply no such diagnostic substrate -- an embodied agent that issued an invalid action and one that lacked an API workflow are both reported only as unsolved -- so recovery recipes treat all failures alike and append reflection, retrieve more examples or run a broad playbook. That produces three concrete costs: an intervention chosen without diagnosis often cannot address the failure at hand, irrelevant procedures actively interfere (long manuals mix incompatible workflow rules, demonstrations for one failure mode degrade another), and triggering everything on every failure inflates environment steps, retrieval budget and tokens whether or not the evidence was needed.

## Contributions

- Recasts agent self-correction as diagnosis-first: a development-failure profile restricts which recovery interventions are admissible before any decision about how much evidence to spend.
- A frozen, verifier-selected success-cost recovery harness instantiated three ways -- an action-validity guard, a procedural fallback chain, and a retrieval-budget policy -- one per benchmark's dominant failure mode.
- A matched-information fairness rerun plus a 2x2 factorial showing the gain is an interaction of plus 46 points between action restriction and matched instruction, with neither component worth more than 4 points alone and privileged information ruled out.
- A three-way diagnosis ablation (correct, generic, mismatched) in which a mismatched intervention falls below a generic playbook on two benchmarks and below the base model on one.
- Cross-task transfer of frozen policies within a domain at small cost, and a preliminary weight-space curriculum giving plus 4.74 points under GRPO.

## Method

Development failures are used to recover part of the compiler's role that these tasks lack. A failure is treated as evidence about the dominant bottleneck of a task family rather than as a request for more context, and the output is a recovery harness: a frozen policy linking a diagnosed failure mode to a restricted set of admissible interventions -- an action-validity guard, a procedural API source, a local induction rule, or a retrieval-demonstration budget. Selection over that restricted policy class is verifier-driven on a success-cost criterion, and the policy is frozen before test evaluation. The causal order is the point: first determine what kind of failure can be repaired, then decide how much recovery evidence to spend. On the embodied benchmark the harness is a deterministic diagnosis-aware rule scorer that ranks each admissible command by a sum of goal, phase, search and training-prior terms minus conflict and loop terms, keeping the top twelve; all terms come from the task description and training-set priors and none from test labels or environment-provided correct actions.

## Results

Three benchmarks, three base models. On the embodied benchmark with one backbone, macro success goes from 40.13 percent (base) and 52.24 (the strongest prompt-adaptation baseline) to 91.94; the pattern repeats on two other backbones (56.90 to 94.90 and 58.00 to 96.33). On the multi-application benchmark, average goal completion goes from 18.32/6.81 base to 74.90/58.86 on one backbone, though on Test-Challenge the margins narrow and one baseline is competitive or better on some metrics with another backbone. On financial extraction, macro accuracy reaches 94.50 against 80.50, notably without using answer labels during adaptation where several baselines do. Confidence intervals from resamples shared across methods do not overlap those of the baselines, and paired t-tests and exact McNemar tests survive Holm correction across 56 scenarios. The decomposition is what makes the result interpretable, and the authors run it against the obvious objection that their guard sees privileged admissibility information. Under a matched-information rerun on the full 134-task unseen split with identical observations, the full admissible action set and a 50-step budget: giving the base agent the same parsed metadata moves it only 39.55 to 43.28, so information access is not the driver; restricting a baseline to a random top-12 action view collapses it from 54.48 to 25.37, so restriction alone is not free and can hurt; diagnosis as a bare label without the ranked recovery operator stays at 38.81, base level; and only the ranked recovery operator reaches 89-90 percent while cutting invalid actions per episode from 1.709 to 0.575 and steps from 35.25 to 16.50. A 2x2 factorial isolates it further: the recovery prompt on the full action set is worth minus 0.75 points, the ranked action view without the prompt plus 3.73, forcing the guard's top-1 command with no model in the loop reaches only 40.33 percent, and the two together are worth plus 49.26 -- an interaction of plus 46.27 points. So the effect lives in the match between restriction and instruction, in neither component alone. The diagnosis ablation makes the same point across benchmarks: the correct diagnosis gives 91.94, 70.24 and 94.50 on the three, a generic playbook gives 52.24, 61.90 and 80.50, and a mismatched intervention gives 52.24, 64.88 and 37.75 -- so on two of three, a mismatched intervention is worse than a generic one and on finance it is worse than the base model. Frozen policies transfer across task pairs with small losses (89.50 against 90.00 target-tuned; 96.00 against 99.00; 90.30 on the unseen split). Retrieval budget is non-monotonic: k=8 and k=16 slightly reduce tag accuracy against smaller budgets, and the distilled policy averages 1.5 retrievals. Cumulative-solve curves show more episodes solved at every step budget, not only at the largest. A preliminary weight-space probe using a DARC-derived two-stage curriculum on an 8B model gives plus 4.74 points with GRPO and plus 2.19 with online self-distillation, which the authors call a proof of concept.

## Limitations

The authors frame theirs as future work: the diagnosis is static and per-task-family, so instance-level routing for mixed-mode failures is not supported; policy distillation is not sample-efficient; and the comparison library is narrow. They explicitly mark the weight-space extension as single-seed with modest absolute gains and not a verified recipe, and note that the matched-information rerun's numbers are not directly comparable to a differently selected frozen cascade elsewhere in the paper. Reader-visible additions: the diagnosis is performed by the authors from development failures rather than automatically, so what is validated is that a correctly matched harness helps enormously, not that the matching can be discovered without human analysis of each new task family -- the three harnesses (action-validity guard, procedural fallback chain, retrieval budget) are three hand-identified bottlenecks. The embodied gain is largely a restriction of the action space to state-compatible commands, which is a strong prior about that environment. Baselines vary in whether they use answer labels, and the paper tabulates this rather than equalising it. The largest and most-analysed gains are on the benchmark where a single dominant failure mode exists; the multi-application benchmark, where failures are mixed, is where the margins are smallest and a baseline sometimes wins.

## Why it matters here

- **test-time-scaling**: The clearest statement in the archive that inference-time compute is not one knob. The ablation table separates three things usually bundled as 'give the agent more context': information access is worth 3.7 points, action-space restriction alone is worth 3.7 and can be worth minus 29 when unmatched, a diagnosis label alone is worth nothing, and the matched combination is worth 49 -- an interaction of 46 points that neither component predicts. That is a direct measurement of the archive's suspicion that scaling the amount of evidence at inference is the wrong axis, and that matching the intervention to the failure is the right one. The diagnosis ablation adds the sharper form: on two of three benchmarks a mismatched intervention scores no better than a generic playbook, and on the third it drops 43 points below the generic one and below the base model, so wrong recovery evidence is actively harmful rather than merely wasted. The retrieval-budget curve is the same shape as the archive's other non-monotonicity results -- k=16 is worse than k=2 -- and the distilled policy converges on 1.5 retrievals. Finally, the cumulative-solve curve shows the gain appearing at every step budget rather than only at large ones, which is what distinguishes a better policy from one that merely got more compute. The caveat to carry with all of this is that the diagnoses are hand-identified per task family, so the paper demonstrates the value of matching without demonstrating that matching can be found automatically.

## Abstract

Self-correction is particularly useful when a failure constrains the next repair. Coding agents benefit from this property because compilers, tests, and execution traces turn many failures into typed recovery signals, but broad language-agent tasks often expose only a coarse task failure. This creates a tension for generic recovery playbooks: they broaden the agent's context precisely when the system needs a narrower repair interface, mixing incompatible signals for invalid actions, missing procedures, and strict-format errors. Our insight is that development-set failures can recover part of the missing diagnostic substrate by deciding which recovery interventions are admissible before test-time correction. We propose DARC, a diagnosis-guided recovery harness that profiles task-family failure modes, prunes mismatched interventions from a shared recovery library, and freezes a verifier-selected success-cost policy for deployment. This causal order makes correction selective: the harness first determines what kind of failure can be repaired, then decides how much recovery evidence to spend. In ALFWorld, AppWorld, and XBRL Finance, the same protocol yields an action-validity harness, a procedural-recovery fallback, and a format-precision retrieval policy; in each evaluated setting it improves average task performance over base agents and broad playbooks while reducing environment steps or retrieval budget. Our experiments show that failures need not trigger uniformly more context: DARC turns self-correction from prompt expansion into recovery-interface design. DARC provides a practical route toward more reliable agents in domains where compiler-like feedback is absent: making failures actionable before making contexts larger.
